rewrite.title: AI Search Visibility: A Practical Guide for Business Owners
rewrite.markdown:
An AI answer can mention your business without sending a customer. It can also send a customer without giving you a neat attribution report.

Build for both realities: publish information worth using, make it accessible and measure the business response. There is no reliable shortcut that turns a rewritten paragraph into a guaranteed recommendation.

## What you are trying to improve

AI-search visibility means a system can find, understand and sometimes reference useful information about your business. Different products retrieve and present information differently. A result in one product is not proof of visibility everywhere.

Start with customer decisions: what you do, who it fits, how the work proceeds, what evidence supports your claims and what someone should do next. A local business also needs consistent location and service information.

## Check each discovery route

| System | Practical check | Important limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Google AI Overviews and AI Mode | Page is indexable, indexed and eligible for a Search snippet | Eligibility does not guarantee a supporting link |
| ChatGPT search | Search crawler can access the public page | Search access and model-training preferences are separate |
| Bing and Copilot | Important pages are discoverable and current | Citation reporting is not a sales report |
| Perplexity | Public search crawler can fetch the page | A user-requested fetch differs from routine crawling |

Google says [normal SEO practices apply to its AI features](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features). It does not require special AI schema or a new text file. Check robots rules, response headers, internal links and the actual HTML before adding another file to the site.

OpenAI documents [separate search and training crawlers](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/bots). Perplexity likewise [describes its search crawler and user fetcher separately](https://docs.perplexity.ai/docs/resources/perplexity-crawlers). Ask the person managing your hosting to check genuine access if security controls appear to block a crawler. A changed browser user-agent string is not proof that the real bot can get through.

## Make the business and its evidence clear

Use the same accurate business identity across your website and legitimate profiles. Identify authors and their actual roles. Describe services in language a buyer would use, and keep qualifications, office claims and results supported by evidence.

Structured data can describe an article, its author, the organization and the page relationships. It must agree with the visible page. Adding a schema property does not make an unsupported claim true.

## Write answers that survive being read out of context

An answer should identify the subject, explain the condition and state any limit that changes the recommendation. Avoid vague references such as “this always works” when the preceding paragraph supplies an essential exception.

For example, a useful platform answer is: “Astro itself does not use PHP. If WordPress remains the editing system, that WordPress installation still needs PHP maintenance.” The second sentence prevents a misleading summary. Our [WordPress and Astro guide](/blog/wordpress-php-security-moving-to-astro/) explains the business choices.

Use tables for comparisons, numbered steps for procedures and diagrams for relationships. Keep their essential meaning in HTML text as well. Microsoft’s [AI-search content guidance](https://about.ads.microsoft.com/en/blog/post/october-2025/optimizing-your-content-for-inclusion-in-ai-search-answers) specifically recommends clear structure and cautions against putting critical information only in images or PDFs.

## Organize topics around the services you sell

Your blog pillars are categories aligned with primary services or product collections. A guide belongs inside the relevant category. It can connect to related articles and the commercial page without pretending that every reader is ready to buy.

For a reporting business, distinct articles might explain metric definitions, source preparation and dashboard evaluation. Each should solve a different problem. Use the [content hub workbook](/blog/build-a-content-hub-people-can-use/) to map those relationships before commissioning more content.

## Run a small, repeatable visibility review

Choose questions customers actually ask. Record the exact prompt, product, date, any supplied location, cited URLs and whether the answer describes your business accurately. Repeat the same questions later, preserving the earlier observations.

This is a sample, not a census. Wording, account context, location and product changes can alter answers. Do not turn one favorable response into an “AI ranking” claim.

Where available, [Bing AI Performance](https://blogs.bing.com/webmaster/2026/2/Introducing-AI-Performance-in-Bing-Webmaster-Tools-Public-Preview/) adds citation evidence. Keep it separate from identifiable referral visits, valid inquiries and qualified leads. Google’s [June 2026 announcement](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2026/06/gen-ai-performance-reports) describes dedicated generative-AI visibility reports alongside overall performance reporting. Inspect the reports available in your property and preserve their definitions; do not infer separate AI clicks or leads from an impressions figure.

## A useful first-month plan

First, inspect your key service pages and business details. Next, repair access problems and unsupported claims. Then improve the answers customers need most, with reviewed examples and relevant internal links. Finally, record search visibility and real inquiries against the starting point.

Assign an owner to each correction and keep unresolved facts visible in your internal working record. Do not publish guesses to complete a checklist.

Our [generative search service](/services/ai-search-optimization/) addresses discoverability and observed citations. [Business intelligence](/services/business-intelligence/) connects the evidence to commercial decisions. Keep those jobs distinct enough that you can tell whether either is working.

## Keep a review record

[Download the fillable search review workbook](/downloads/search-review-workbook.pdf). It includes a worked comparison, space for your sources and decisions, and 12 acceptance checks. Keep unresolved questions with an owner and review date.

rewrite.title: Google Shopping Management: Fix the Feed Before Scaling
rewrite.markdown:
Increasing a Shopping budget gives an existing system more room to spend. It does not repair an incorrect price, an unavailable product or a purchase event counted twice.

Before changing spend, establish three things: the products are eligible, measurement is dependable and the business can afford the acquisition cost. You need access to Merchant Center, Google Ads and the store's actual order and cost records.

## Verify the catalog first

Review account and item issues in Merchant Center. Compare priority products with their landing pages: item, variant, image, price, currency, availability, delivery and returns. Google's [product data specification](https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/7052112) is the reference for required fields and exceptions.

Fix mismatches in the system that owns the information. Use the [Shopify connection checklist](/blog/shopify-google-merchant-center-checklist/) when that is your platform. Keep a record of affected item IDs so you can verify the next successful update.

## Choose a campaign for the job

Standard Shopping and Performance Max are different campaign types. [Performance Max](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/10724817) can serve across Google's advertising inventory; it is not simply another name for Shopping. Its broader scope matters when you interpret a campaign total.

Choose based on the business objective, available creative, conversion measurement, catalog and control needs. There is no universal rule that every store should move its entire catalog into one campaign type. Read the current account options before making a migration and document what reporting or controls will change.

## Calculate what an order can support

Revenue divided by ad spend is return on ad spend, or ROAS. It does not subtract product costs, fulfilment or returns. A high ROAS can still accompany poor economics.

Illustrative example: an order produces $100 in net sales. Product cost is $35, variable fulfilment and payment costs are $15, and expected return-related costs are $5. That leaves $45 before acquisition and fixed overhead. If the business needs $20 of that contribution to remain, the initial acquisition allowance is $25. Confirm the cost definitions with the person responsible for the accounts; do not count the same return twice.

Our [order acquisition worksheet](/blog/what-can-you-afford-to-spend-on-an-order/) provides the fuller calculation, including uncertainty. An allowance is a planning constraint, not a prediction that ads can obtain orders at that cost.

## Define a test before changing the budget

Write down the eligible product group, conversion goal, cost limit, review date and conditions that stop the test. Include inventory constraints and the time needed for conversions to arrive. Do not promise a statistically reliable result from a small arbitrary budget.

For a store comparing two product groups, keep the comparison clear: similar dates, known promotions and consistent cost definitions. If one group has much higher returns or lower margin, revenue alone is not a fair comparison.

![Campaign review sequence: define the outcome, check the journey, set limits, verify tracking and review business results.](/media/blog-review/campaign-checkpoints.svg)

## Reconcile the reported purchases

Take an authorized test transaction or a known order and verify its value, currency and event identity. Review conversion settings, attribution windows and delays with the account owner. Do not add Google, Meta and other platform-attributed orders together as unique store orders.

Use the store's records to establish total business activity. Use platform reports to understand delivery under their stated definitions. Neither source should silently replace the other.

## Decide whether to expand, repair or stop

At the review date, check eligibility, spending, stock, purchases and contribution. A delivery problem calls for diagnosis. An uneconomic offer calls for a business decision. Incomplete data calls for an explicit uncertainty note, not an optimistic result.

[Download the campaign test brief](/downloads/campaign-test-brief.pdf). Record the decision and what evidence would change it. Increase spend only within an agreed limit, then review whether the economics hold as the campaign reaches more buyers.

rewrite.markdown:
A Shopify launch is ready when a customer can find the right product, understand it and complete an order—and your team can verify what happened. A finished homepage does not establish any of those things.

Use this checklist before a new store, migration or major theme release. You will need access to Shopify, your domain settings and the people responsible for product information and measurement. Search Console and Merchant Center checks require access to those properties too.

## Decide what must work at launch

List your priority collections and products. Include an ordinary product, a product with variants, a discounted item and an unavailable item. Test each relevant template rather than assuming the homepage represents the store.

Keep a launch sheet with these columns: URL, test, expected result, observed result, evidence, owner and release decision. A blocked checkout or incorrect selling price stops release. A missing optional description improvement can have a named follow-up date.

## Check the address and discovery rules

Confirm the primary domain and HTTPS. Open the www and non-www versions and any old store addresses; verify they resolve to the intended destination. For a migration, test old product and collection links individually against the redirect map.

Shopify includes [built-in SEO features](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/promoting-marketing/seo/seo-overview), including canonical tags and sitemap generation. Those defaults still need inspection after theme and app changes. A canonical identifies the preferred version of equivalent content; it is not a way to hide a genuinely different product.

Check that public launch pages are not password protected or marked noindex. Keep staging and private areas excluded. Review the [generated sitemap](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/promoting-marketing/seo/find-site-map), then submit it through the correct Search Console property. Submission does not guarantee indexing.

## Walk from a collection to a purchase

Start on a phone. Find a collection through navigation, choose a product, select its size or colour and add it to the cart. Confirm that the selected variant, image, price and availability agree through checkout.

On each collection, explain what belongs there and provide useful filters. Do not create several almost identical collections merely to target slight wording differences. Product pages should state the facts a buyer needs: dimensions, materials, compatibility, contents, delivery and returns, as applicable.

Give images useful descriptions. Describe the product or information shown; do not fill alt text with every search phrase you hope to rank for.

## Check product information in three places

Compare the visible page, its structured data and any Merchant Center listing. Check price, currency, availability, variant selection and destination. A valid schema test does not establish that the values are correct.

Google's [product variant guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/structured-data/product-variants) distinguishes single-page and multi-page implementations. Ask the developer to verify the pattern the store actually uses. Do not copy a canonical rule from a different variant model.

For feed setup, follow the separate [Shopify and Merchant Center checklist](/blog/shopify-google-merchant-center-checklist/). For an established store with indexing problems, use the [Shopify repair guide](/blog/shopify-seo-problems-real-fixes/).

## Worked launch check

Imagine a store selling linen shirts. This is an illustrative test, not a client result.

| Check | Expected result | Action if it fails |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Open the blue, medium variant link | Blue and medium are selected at the advertised price | Fix selection or destination before promotion |
| Add that variant to the cart | The same SKU, quantity and price appear | Resolve the cart mismatch before launch |
| Follow the delivery and returns links | Terms cover the actual product and destination | Correct the policy or delivery configuration |
| Complete an authorized test order | Order record and purchase event carry the same value and currency | Investigate measurement before using it for ad decisions |
| Open an old product link | It reaches the relevant replacement without a chain | Repair the redirect map |

Use a test payment method approved for the store, and remove test records from business reporting where appropriate. Do not place unapproved live orders.

## Validate after release

Repeat the checks on the public domain. Confirm checkout, forms and tracking consent behaviour. Review Search Console for crawl and indexing changes; compare Merchant Center issues with the inspected products. Use the [GA4 event validation guide](/blog/ga4-ecommerce-event-validation/) to reconcile a known order rather than assuming a dashboard proves tracking works.

Save the launch sheet with its evidence. [Download the search review workbook](/downloads/search-review-workbook.pdf) for the URL, owner and follow-up checks. Keep the product-specific expectations above alongside it.

rewrite.title: The Four Pillars of SEO: A Practical Review
rewrite.markdown:
Technical access, useful content, credible authority and usable pages provide a useful way to organize SEO work. They are planning categories, not four scores supplied by Google.

Keep that framework separate from your blog pillars. A blog pillar is a category aligned with a primary service or product collection; it houses related articles. An individual guide belongs inside a category. The [content hub guide](/blog/build-a-content-hub-people-can-use/) shows that structure.

## Technical access: can the important page be found?

Choose a real service or collection page. Check that it loads successfully, can be reached through an ordinary internal link and is intended to be indexed. Inspect its canonical and Google's indexed version where Search Console access is available.

Google's [technical requirements](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/technical) establish eligibility, not a promise of indexing or ranking. A technically accessible page can still lack a useful answer.

## Content: does it help the buyer decide?

Read the page without its navigation or sales pitch. Can a prospective customer understand the offer, its fit, important limitations and the next step? Explain the questions that would otherwise stop an inquiry or purchase.

For a reporting service, that might mean describing required data access, the decisions a dashboard supports and who maintains it. For a product collection, selection criteria may matter more than a long introduction. Google's [people-first guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) is a useful quality reference; it is not a mandatory article template.

## Authority: what supports the claim?

Use relevant work, named authors, primary references and genuine qualifications. Keep numerical results tied to their period, scope and source. Remove a claim if the business cannot substantiate it.

Useful recognition and links should arise from relevant work or participation. Buying links to manipulate rankings or manufacturing reviews introduces a different problem. Read Google's [spam policies](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies) before accepting an agency's link package.

## Usability: can someone complete the task?

Test the page on a phone and with a keyboard. Read the text, open the navigation, inspect supporting images and complete the intended inquiry or purchase journey. Check errors, labels, contrast and layout movement.

A performance score is one diagnostic. It does not establish that an offer makes sense or that a form reaches the right inbox. Keep the [technical review](/blog/technical-seo-ten-fixes-that-move-rankings/) connected to the actual task.

## Worked example: choose the first repair

Imagine a consultancy whose service page receives search visits but few valid inquiries. The page loads correctly and is indexed. Its copy never states which systems it works with, and the mobile form fails after submission.

| Finding | First action | Acceptance check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Broken form | Repair submission and confirmation | Authorized test reaches the intended inbox |
| Unclear fit | Explain supported engagement types and requirements | A reader can identify whether to inquire |
| Unsupported result claim | Add verified evidence or remove the claim | Public wording matches retained proof |

This example does not establish why inquiries are low. It identifies observable defects worth fixing before commissioning more articles or links.

## Turn the review into a small backlog

Record the page, evidence, buyer consequence, owner and validation for each issue. Resolve access and task-breaking faults first, then prioritize improvements against the business objective. Keep a baseline so later comparisons do not rely on memory.

[Download the search review workbook](/downloads/search-review-workbook.pdf). Use the four areas as prompts, and close an item only when its specific acceptance check passes.

rewrite.title: Technical SEO: Ten Checks Before You Expand the Site
rewrite.markdown:
Technical SEO should leave important public pages accessible, understandable and usable. It cannot compensate for an offer nobody wants or an article that does not answer its question.

Start with a sample covering the homepage, a service or collection page, a product where relevant, an article and a form. You need site-management access or a developer who can make the changes, plus Search Console access for Google's indexed evidence. Keep private routes private.

## Ten checks and their acceptance tests

| Check | What to inspect | Evidence that the repair worked |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Preferred domain | HTTPS and alternate domain redirects | Public links resolve to the intended host |
| Redirects | Old URLs, loops and unnecessary chains | Each mapped old page reaches its relevant destination |
| Indexing controls | Robots rules, noindex and response headers | Public pages are eligible; private pages stay excluded |
| Canonical URLs | Equivalent versions and conflicting tags | One consistent preferred equivalent URL is declared |
| Useful performance | Loading, interaction and layout stability | Comparable tests improve without breaking the task |
| Sitemap | Canonical public URLs and response status | Listed pages exist and are intended for indexing |
| Rendered content | Answers, links and headings | Important information is present in accessible HTML |
| Structured data | Types, values and visible claims | Valid markup agrees with the public page |
| Internal discovery | Navigation and contextual links | Important pages have relevant crawlable links |
| Error handling | Missing pages and failed requests | Correct responses and helpful recovery paths |

These are checks, not ten guaranteed ranking improvements. Prioritize a demonstrated blocker over a cosmetic warning.

## Do not confuse crawling with indexing

A robots.txt rule controls crawling. A noindex directive controls indexing when the crawler can read it. Blocking a page in robots.txt can prevent the crawler from seeing a noindex directive. Google's [robots introduction](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots/intro) explains the distinction.

Do not open private content to solve an indexing warning. Establish what is meant to be public, then apply the appropriate access and search controls.

## Use canonicals for equivalent content

A canonical is a preferred-version signal, not a redirect and not a guarantee that Google selects the same URL. A permanent redirect is appropriate when an old address is retired and has a relevant replacement.

Read Google's [canonical guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/consolidate-duplicate-urls), then use the [duplicate-content decision guide](/blog/duplicate-content-isnt-a-penalty-but-its-a-tax/) for examples. Do not canonicalize distinct service pages to the homepage to make a report look cleaner.

## Worked investigation: a missing service page

Suppose a new service page is absent from search. First open it directly and check its response. Then inspect its indexing controls, canonical, internal links and sitemap entry. Use Search Console's indexed record and live inspection for their different purposes.

If a launch template accidentally contains noindex, remove it only from the intended public pages. Deploy, inspect the public HTML again and request indexing through an authorized property when appropriate. Record the correction date. A successful live test proves current access, not immediate inclusion in search.

## Check the task after changing the template

Template repairs affect more than the example URL. Recheck neighbouring pages, mobile navigation, forms and structured data. Use Google's [page experience guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/page-experience) to put performance in context rather than treating a perfect laboratory score as the entire goal.

Keep an owner, rollback route and acceptance test for every change. [Download the search review workbook](/downloads/search-review-workbook.pdf) to retain the evidence and follow-up date.

rewrite.title: Local SEO: Build an Accurate, Useful Local Presence
rewrite.markdown:
Local search starts with a real business operating in a real place. A city name added to every heading cannot make an address eligible, shorten the distance to a searcher or establish a reputation.

Before editing listings, gather the authoritative business name, customer-facing phone, website, operating arrangements and any actual visitor hours. Resolve disagreements between records instead of copying whichever directory appears first.

## Understand what local visibility depends on

Google describes local results in terms of [relevance, distance and prominence](https://support.google.com/business/answer/7091). Complete information helps Google understand the business; location and recognition also matter. No agency can buy a better organic local position from Google.

Record the query, date, device and location context when checking results. A normal web search is not a controlled local rank grid. “Miami” in a query does not prove the searcher is physically in Miami.

## Establish profile eligibility before editing an address

Follow Google's [business representation rules](https://support.google.com/business/answer/3038177). Storefront, service-area and hybrid businesses have different practical requirements. A mailing address or virtual office is not automatically an eligible customer-facing location.

If customers are not served at an address, review the applicable service-area rules. Do not invent opening hours or staff presence to make a listing look complete. Where access or facts are unresolved, prepare a correction record and leave the external edit pending.

## Build a page that answers local buying questions

A useful city page explains services available, how an engagement works, relevant evidence and how to inquire. Give it genuine local substance. Do not generate dozens of nearly identical city-and-service combinations.

For a business based in Panama City and serving Miami, describe that arrangement directly. Relevant Miami work can support the relationship without claiming a permanently staffed Miami reception desk. ZINC's [Panama City](/locations/panama-city/) and [Miami](/locations/miami/) pages distinguish operating base from service coverage.

## Reconcile the website and profiles

Compare business name, address where applicable, phone, website, category, hours and profile links. Record each discrepancy with its source and a verified replacement. Structured data should reflect the same established facts; it does not validate an uncertain address.

Keep an old URL's redirect working when a landing page changes. Check the profile destination on a phone and test the inquiry route. Use separate locations only when actual operations justify them.

## Ask actual customers for honest reviews

Use a consistent invitation after a suitable completed interaction: “If you would like to share your experience, you can leave an honest review here.” Provide the correct profile link and make the request optional.

Do not offer incentives, write the review for the customer or send only satisfied customers to the public review page. Google's [prohibited content policy](https://support.google.com/contributionpolicy/answer/7400114) addresses fake engagement. Resolve customer problems through normal service, independently of whether a review is changed.

## Worked monthly review

Imagine a marine contractor serving several nearby communities. Its phone is correct on the website but outdated in one directory, a service page promises work the team no longer offers, and the inquiry form omits a project-location field.

Correct the verified phone, revise the service scope and add the location question if it helps qualification. Record which sources changed and verify their public readback. Then compare valid inquiries and service fit over time. Do not claim the directory correction caused every subsequent lead.

Use available profile performance, Search Console and inquiry records for their separate purposes. Track qualified opportunities as well as visibility. [Download the search review workbook](/downloads/search-review-workbook.pdf) for a record of the observations, owners and unresolved facts.

rewrite.title: A Content Marketing Plan Connected to Sales
rewrite.markdown:
A publishing calendar tells you when an article is due. It does not tell you why a customer would need it.

Build the plan around the services or products you actually sell, the questions customers ask before buying and the evidence your team can provide. Then assign the writing. This order saves a remarkable amount of editorial wandering.

## Start with one commercial priority

Choose a service or product collection the business wants to support. Confirm that it has a useful commercial page and that someone can handle the resulting enquiries. More traffic to an unclear offer is not much of a plan.

Before commissioning anything, gather the current pages, recent customer questions, available Search Console data and approved examples. Separate observed customer needs from assumptions. If you have no search data yet, say so and start with documented enquiries rather than inventing demand.

## Define the pillar, category and articles

A pillar is a blog category aligned with a primary service or product collection. It houses the articles on that main topic. A substantial guide can belong to the category, but it is not the category itself.

The service or collection page explains the offer. The category helps readers browse the related advice. Individual articles answer distinct questions. Link between those pages when the next step helps the reader; do not make every article repeat the same sales paragraph.

For the complete architecture and printable planning tools, use our [content hub guide](/blog/build-a-content-hub-people-can-use/).

![The primary service aligns with a blog category that houses distinct supporting articles.](/media/content-hub/pillar-map.svg)

## Worked example: a business reporting service

This is an illustrative plan, not a claim about client results.

| Page | Reader’s question | Useful next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Business intelligence service | Can someone help us build reliable reporting? | Explain scope and start an enquiry |
| Business intelligence blog category | What should we understand before commissioning reporting? | Browse the related guides |
| KPI definitions article | Why do our reports disagree on revenue? | Complete a metric definition sheet |
| Data preparation article | What records should we supply? | Gather sources, permissions and sample records |
| Dashboard review article | How do we check that a report is useful? | Test one decision against the underlying records |

The three articles have different jobs. One resolves a definition problem, another prepares the project, and the third helps assess the result. They need different examples, not three versions of an introduction to dashboards.

## Write the brief before the draft

For each assignment, record the reader, main question, intended action, category, evidence, section outline and links. Name a factual reviewer. Mark information you still need; do not quietly fill it with plausible claims.

A good brief specifies a usable deliverable. For the revenue example, that means a completed definition showing gross versus net revenue, discounts, refunds, tax, currency and date basis. See the [content brief walkthrough](/blog/content-briefs-search-intent-internal-links/) for a filled example.

Google’s [people-first content guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) is a useful editorial check: the page should help its intended reader and contribute something beyond a restatement of other pages. There is no useful word-count target for every assignment.

## Put distribution and maintenance on the same plan

Choose where each article will be useful: a relevant sales follow-up, an existing customer email, a category archive or another article answering the preceding question. Obtain any necessary communication approval before sending material.

Set a maintenance trigger. A product specification change, revised platform documentation or recurring customer misunderstanding can justify an update. A fresh date alone cannot.

Start with a manageable sequence: inventory existing material, repair the commercial page and category, publish the most useful answers, then review what readers still need. Keep the publishing frequency within the team’s actual capacity.

## Measure progress without inventing attribution

Use Search Console for the queries and pages that appear in Google Search. Its [Performance report](https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/7576553) is not a complete record of people or sales. Use your inquiry or sales records to assess whether the resulting conversations fit the business.

For the example, track visits to the reporting service, valid reporting enquiries and questions raised during sales calls. Keep assisted visits separate from new leads. One customer reading three articles remains one customer.

At the review, decide whether to improve an existing answer, produce the next missing guide or stop an assignment that no longer has a purpose. Use the [BI category](/blog/category/business-intelligence/) for related measurement guidance and the [channel planning guide](/blog/seven-digital-channels-which-to-skip/) to place content alongside other marketing activity.

## Before the first article goes live

- The category matches a real service or collection.
- The commercial page explains the offer and the enquiry path works.
- Every article has a distinct reader question and reviewed evidence.
- Examples are real and approved, or clearly labelled illustrative.
- Category, article and commercial links lead to useful next pages.
- A person owns the review date and the measurement definitions.

If you cannot identify the decision an article helps someone make, improve the brief before adding it to the calendar.

rewrite.title: When a Web Design Trend Is Worth Using
rewrite.markdown:
A design trend earns its place when it makes the website clearer, more usable or more distinctive in a way the business can maintain. Looking current is not a sufficient acceptance test.

Start with the page's job. A product page needs to support selection and purchase. A consultancy page needs to explain fit and earn an inquiry. A reporting screen needs to support a decision. The same visual treatment will not serve all three equally well.

## Judge the treatment against the task

| Treatment | Useful application | What to test |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Large typography | Clear offer and deliberate hierarchy | Long titles and small-screen wrapping |
| Dark presentation | Appropriate brand or viewing context | Text, controls and graphics in both themes |
| Scroll effects | Explain relationships or section changes | Reading remains immediate; reduced motion works |
| Custom illustration | Explain something a photograph cannot | Topic accuracy, legibility and adjacent text |
| Personalization | Help a visitor with a known need | Consent, fallback and incorrect assumptions |

An effect that obscures a heading, traps scrolling or delays a form needs repair even if the animation itself is technically impressive.

## Inspect a complete journey

Choose a task and follow it from entry to completion on desktop and mobile. For an inquiry page, read the offer, find evidence, open the form, make an error and recover. Check that submission reaches the intended recipient through an authorized test.

Use a keyboard as well as a pointer. Check visible focus, labels and readable contrast. The [WCAG quick reference](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/quickref/) provides the relevant accessibility requirements; passing an automated scan alone does not establish usability.

## Worked decision: keep the diagonal, protect the copy

Consider a decorative diagonal background behind a service section. Its purpose is to connect the composition as the page scrolls. Keep it behind the content, preserve text contrast throughout the scroll range and avoid making the reading itself depend on an animation completing.

Test short and tall screens, both colour themes and reduced-motion settings. If the effect clips a heading or produces horizontal scrolling, repair its positioning or bounds. The design can remain distinctive without asking visitors to work around it.

## Check performance without sacrificing clarity

Measure the templates customers actually use, including large images and interactive controls. Compare tests under similar conditions and distinguish laboratory measurements from real-user evidence. Google's [Core Web Vitals guidance](https://web.dev/articles/vitals) explains the loading, interaction and layout-stability measures.

Do not blur a useful product image simply to improve one score. Use appropriate dimensions and responsive delivery, then inspect the visible result. A faster page that hides important details has traded one problem for another.

## Write a design acceptance note

For each proposed change, record the user task, expected benefit, content requirements, mobile behaviour and validation. A useful note might read: “Keep the product image sharp at normal viewing sizes; display size selection before the purchase button; preserve keyboard operation; verify selected variant through checkout.”

That gives the designer and developer something concrete to deliver. Compare behaviour and real outcomes after release while accounting for other changes. Use the [landing-page checklist](/blog/paid-media-landing-page-checklist/) when the page supports a campaign, or the [Shopify launch checklist](/blog/shopify-seo-launch-checklist/) for a store release.

rewrite.title: Shopify SEO Problems: Diagnose Before You Change
rewrite.markdown:
An SEO audit can find hundreds of warnings without identifying the problem costing the store orders. Start with a specific symptom and a small set of affected pages. Then test the explanation before changing the whole catalog.

You need access to the store, Search Console and the people maintaining the theme and product data. Merchant Center access is useful when the problem also affects product listings. Record recent releases, app changes and catalog imports before troubleshooting.

## Separate visibility from buying problems

If a collection receives fewer search appearances, inspect indexing and the relevant queries. If appearances hold but clicks fall, inspect the results and competing offers. If visits hold but orders fall, examine availability, price, checkout and measurement.

These patterns guide investigation; they do not prove a cause. Compare equivalent periods and account for promotions and seasonal demand. See the [query-and-page review](/blog/search-console-query-page-review/) for a manageable starting sample.

## Diagnose the URL problem

A product may be reached through several paths. That is not automatically a fault. Check which URL appears in navigation, the sitemap, the canonical tag and Google's indexed record.

Shopify's [SEO overview](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/promoting-marketing/seo/seo-overview) describes its built-in canonical support. Themes and apps can still introduce conflicting output. Ask a developer to inspect the rendered page before installing another SEO app.

Use Google's [canonical guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/consolidate-duplicate-urls) for equivalent pages. Distinct products need their own treatment. Variant URLs also need to follow the store's actual [single-page or multi-page model](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/structured-data/product-variants).

![Decide whether to keep a distinct page, canonicalize an equivalent version or redirect a retired address.](/media/blog-review/canonical-decisions.svg)

## Give collections a clear buying purpose

Open the collection without reading its SEO title. Can a shopper tell what belongs there, narrow the choices and reach a suitable product? Add useful selection guidance where it answers a real question. Avoid long introductory copy that pushes the products out of reach.

Two collections with similar names may serve different buyers. Compare their product sets and purpose before consolidating them. If they are genuinely redundant, choose a destination, map redirects and update internal links. Preserve a distinct category when it meets a distinct need.

## Repair product facts at their source

Compare the product record, public page, structured data and feed for a sample of affected items. Look for stale price, unavailable variants, misleading images or missing compatibility details. Assign one source owner for each field.

For example, an illustrative blue medium shirt appears as available in a feed while the selected variant is sold out. First establish whether the inventory record, connector or page output is stale. Correct that system and check the next refresh. Rewriting the product title would not repair availability.

## Test performance where customers buy

Check collection, product and cart pages on a phone. Record slow interactions and layout shifts. Use field performance data where available and repeat laboratory tests under comparable conditions; one test score is not a reliable business result.

Before removing an app, establish its purpose and dependencies. Disable or replace it in a safe preview, test the affected functions, and compare performance. Keep reviews, accessibility and purchase controls working.

## Close one repair with evidence

Your repair record should contain the affected URLs, observed defect, proposed change, owner, test and rollback route. After deployment, repeat the original test and check neighbouring products. Then monitor discovery and orders over an appropriate period without attributing every movement to the repair.

[Download the search review workbook](/downloads/search-review-workbook.pdf). For a new release, use the [launch checklist](/blog/shopify-seo-launch-checklist/); for feed errors, use [Merchant Center diagnostics](/blog/merchant-center-feed-diagnostics/).

An update date can explain when Google changed something. It cannot, by itself, explain why your website lost traffic.

This is a source-based review of selected Search changes across 2023–2026, not a study of ranking winners and losers. We have not supplied a controlled dataset that could support that second claim. Keeping the distinction clear makes the history more useful.

## What the dated record establishes

Google’s [ranking update history](https://status.search.google.com/) records announced rollouts. Read the individual entries for the complete dates and scope; the examples below are selected events, not an exhaustive timeline.

| Announcement | Documented event | What a website owner should investigate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 14 September 2023 | Helpful content update began | Whether affected content answers its intended reader’s needs |
| 5 March 2024 | Core update and new spam-policy announcement | Content quality and whether any actual practices conflict with the policies |
| 13 March 2025 | March core update began | Page/query changes across the completed rollout, alongside site changes |
| 21 May 2026 | May core update began | Comparable-period performance and alternative explanations |

Those dates establish timing. They do not establish that every movement during a rollout was caused by the update or that one particular edit will reverse it.

## The 2024 policy changes deserve a careful reading

Google’s [March 2024 announcement](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2024/03/core-update-spam-policies) discussed changes to its core ranking systems and policies concerning expired-domain abuse, scaled-content abuse and site-reputation abuse.

For a business owner, the useful question is whether published pages serve customers and whether the site uses the practices described in the policy. Do not reduce that question to an AI-detector score. A tool guessing how prose was written cannot establish whether the page is accurate, useful or compliant.

Likewise, an ordinary ranking decline is not evidence of a manual penalty. Check the relevant account reports before making that claim.

## Search presentation changed as well

AI answers and other search features can change what a person sees before reaching a website. That is a reason to review search appearances, page traffic and business outcomes separately.

Google’s [AI features documentation](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features) explains eligibility and normal SEO foundations. Its [June 2026 reporting announcement](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2026/06/gen-ai-performance-reports) describes additional generative-AI visibility reports. These developments concern discovery and measurement; they are not a universal explanation for declining revenue.

## How to use the history in an actual review

First, establish when the relevant rollout finished. Google’s [core update guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/core-updates) recommends waiting at least a full week after completion before analyzing the suggested comparison.

Then gather the affected pages, query groups, devices and countries. Compare consistent periods and note seasonality. Add your own release dates: a migration, changed navigation, stock outage or accidental indexing restriction may be more directly actionable than the algorithm announcement.

Keep observations separate from possible causes:

| Observation | Possible explanations | Next evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One service page lost clicks | Demand, competition, changed search appearance, indexing or content changes | Query/page breakdown and URL inspection |
| Most mobile inquiries fell | Form failure, mobile layout, traffic mix or search loss | Test the form and compare traffic sources |
| Product pages disappeared | Availability, canonical changes or indexing restrictions | Inspect representative URLs and recent theme changes |

These are diagnostic examples, not conclusions about a particular site.

## Avoid the retrospective trap

A convincing explanation written after a traffic change is still a hypothesis until the evidence supports it. If you changed titles, internal links, page structure and content together, a later improvement does not reveal which change mattered.

Keep a dated change log and use a measured repair sequence. Fix confirmed defects first. Review useful pages for missing answers and evidence; do not remove good information because a generic update checklist says to shorten everything.

For a current investigation, follow the [core update review](/blog/google-core-update-review/) and [Search Console guide](/blog/google-search-console-the-operators-guide/). For the broader service, [SEO](/services/seo/) should connect technical findings, content quality and business outcomes. The historical record is context for that work, not a substitute for it.

## Keep a review record

[Download the fillable search review workbook](/downloads/search-review-workbook.pdf). It includes a worked comparison, space for your sources and decisions, and 12 acceptance checks. Keep unresolved questions with an owner and review date.

Establish which integration sends the products and who maintains it. A native channel may be sufficient; additional feed software needs a specific reason, such as a catalog requirement the current integration cannot meet. Avoid overlapping sources that overwrite the same fields unpredictably.

Use Shopify's [Google & YouTube channel requirements](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/online-sales-channels/google/requirements) and Google's [product data specification](https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/7052112) for the current requirements. Confirm that the correct Merchant Center account owns the website connection. Check the business identity, domain, target countries and available destinations. Stop if a different account already claims the store; resolve ownership rather than creating another account to work around it.

Open the storefront as a customer. Contact information, checkout, delivery costs and returns must be usable and accurate. Do not copy a generic policy that the business cannot fulfil.

Choose a simple product, a variant product, a sale item and an unavailable item. Record their IDs and compare each across Shopify, the submitted product data and the landing page.

| Field | What to verify |
| --- | --- |
| ID | Stable identifier for the same item across updates |

A smaller budget needs clearer choices, not the same percentage cut applied to every line. Protect the work the business can justify, identify uncertainty and stop paying for activity nobody can explain.

Work with the person responsible for cash and accounts before changing commitments. Bring current spending, contractual obligations, sales records, variable costs and the timing of payments and receipts.

## Separate commitments from decisions you can change

List each item with its owner, purpose, cost, cancellation terms and next decision date. Distinguish an immediate cash saving from a theoretical saving that cannot occur until a contract ends.

Include internal time and the cost of stopping and restarting essential work. Do not assume an apparently free channel has no production or service burden.

## Compare contribution, not just revenue

Revenue does not show how much remains after fulfilling an order. Use a consistent definition of net sales and variable costs, including expected returns where appropriate. Keep fixed overhead and acquisition costs visible rather than subtracting them inconsistently.

Illustrative example: a $100 order leaves $40 after product and variable fulfilment costs. Spending $35 to acquire it leaves $5 before fixed overhead. Whether that is acceptable depends on the business's actual cash needs and reliable repeat-purchase evidence—not an assumed lifetime value.

Use the [order economics worksheet](/blog/what-can-you-afford-to-spend-on-an-order/) to test the calculation. For long sales cycles, examine qualified opportunities and the delay before payment rather than comparing this week's spend only with this week's sales.

## Build a decision sheet

| Item | Evidence to bring | Decision available |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Paid campaign | Spend, valid outcomes, contribution, attribution limits | Continue within a limit, repair or pause |
| Content work | Buyer question, distribution, relevant inquiries, maintenance need | Prioritize useful work or reduce output |
| Software | Active use, dependency, overlap, contract terms | Retain, consolidate or cancel when permitted |
| Measurement repair | Specific missing decision and repair scope | Fund a bounded fix with an acceptance test |
| Customer retention | Permission, engagement, repeat-order economics | Improve a relevant programme without assuming free sales |

Do not label a channel ineffective merely because its source is incomplete. Record the uncertainty and decide whether the cost of resolving it is justified.

## Avoid misleading comparisons

Platform reports use their own conversion and attribution settings. Google's [conversion tracking documentation](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/1722022) and [GA4 attribution guidance](https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/10596866) explain why reported credit needs interpretation.

Do not add several platforms' credited purchases as separate store orders. Keep total sales anchored to the business records, and compare periods with similar trading conditions where possible. Mark promotions, stock shortages and tracking changes.

## Make one bounded decision

Suppose two subscriptions perform the same reporting task, but one also sends a required customer notification. Verify that dependency before cancellation. A useful saving preserves the required workflow and has a tested replacement where necessary.

For a campaign, set the spend limit, review date and conditions that stop it. For content, reduce low-priority production while preserving factual maintenance of important pages. Across-the-board cuts can remove necessary work along with waste.

## Review cash and outcomes together

Record the expected saving, when it takes effect, what could deteriorate and who checks it. Review actual costs and business outcomes after the change. If the evidence contradicts the original assumption, revise the decision.

rewrite.markdown:
A ranking change during an announced update is a reason to investigate. It is not proof that the update caused the change, or that a particular paragraph needs rewriting.

Keep the investigation small enough to understand. You need Search Console access, a record of website changes and relevant business context such as promotions, stock and seasonality.

## Confirm the event and dates

Check the [Google Search Status Dashboard](https://status.search.google.com/) for the event type and rollout dates. Distinguish a core update, a spam update and a serving incident. A social-media volatility screenshot is not the official event record.

Record whether the rollout is complete. Google's [core update guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/core-updates) recommends waiting at least a full week after completion before analysing the impact in Search Console. Fix independently verified faults, such as a broken form or accidental noindex, without pretending they prove an algorithm diagnosis.

## Compare equivalent groups

Compare affected pages and queries across sensible periods, using consistent country, device and search-type filters. Inspect impressions, clicks and position together. Separate brand queries, service pages, articles and product collections where their purposes differ.

Account for reporting delay, low volume and seasonality. A change in average position can reflect a different mix of queries. Review the [Search Console walkthrough](/blog/google-search-console-the-operators-guide/) before treating an aggregate as a page-level explanation.

## Worked example: fewer article clicks, steady inquiries

Imagine informational articles lose clicks while service-page visits and qualified inquiries remain similar. That does not establish that the content is fine or that AI answers caused the decline.

Inspect the affected queries and current results. Check whether demand, the search presentation, competing pages or your own page changed. Review whether the article still provides a useful, accurate answer. Keep the business outcome separate from the visibility diagnosis.

| Observation | Possible explanation | Next evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One template loses indexed pages | Technical release problem | Public HTML and URL Inspection |
| Seasonal queries lose impressions | Demand change | Comparable seasonal periods and query context |
| Clicks fall while appearances hold | Result presentation or competing offers | Actual results and query-level comparison |
| Orders fall across channels | Broader business or measurement issue | Stock, checkout and order records |

These are hypotheses, not automatic conclusions.

## Make a change you can evaluate

If the page has factual errors, missing buying information or broken navigation, repair those defects. Record the reason and deployment date. Avoid changing the title, URL, content, template and internal links all at once merely to demonstrate activity.

Some problems require coordinated changes. In that case, document the bundle and accept that isolating each change's effect will be harder. Preserve useful pages and URLs unless the evidence supports a different treatment.

## Review without promising recovery dates

After a repair, verify the public result first. Then monitor discovery and relevant business outcomes over an appropriate period. Google's guidance does not promise that every change produces recovery at the next update.

rewrite.markdown:
Search Console tells you how your website appears in Google Search. It does not tell you whether an inquiry became a good customer.

Use it to find the next useful question, then connect the answer to your website and business records. Opening every chart at once rarely improves the diagnosis.

## Before you start

Confirm access to the correct property and identify its coverage. A Domain property and a URL-prefix property can include different versions of a site. Ask the owner for appropriate access rather than sharing credentials.

Write one question: “Why did visits to our reporting service fall?” is specific enough to investigate. Save the page URL, date range, device, country and search type with the review so the next comparison means the same thing.

Google’s [getting-started guide](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/monitor-debug/search-console-start) explains the major reports. Use them for different jobs:

| Question | Starting point | What it cannot establish alone |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Did search appearances change? | Performance | Whether the visitor bought |
| Is this URL indexed? | URL Inspection | Whether it will rank well |
| Are many pages excluded? | Page indexing | Whether every exclusion is a defect |
| Did Google read the sitemap? | Sitemaps | Whether every listed page was indexed |
| Is a manual action recorded? | Manual actions | The cause of every traffic decline |

## Compare the same page over sensible periods

In Performance, select Web search and filter to the page or page group you are investigating. Compare complete periods with similar weekday coverage. Use a year-over-year comparison too when the business is seasonal. Note promotions, site changes and incomplete recent data.

Review clicks, impressions, click-through rate and average position together. Google’s [metric definitions](https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/7042828) explain that these describe search-result appearances and interactions. They are not unique customer counts. A site-wide average can change because the mix of queries changed.

## Worked example: fewer clicks, more appearances

The following figures are illustrative, not ZINC or client results.

| Period | Impressions | Clicks | Click-through rate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Previous complete four weeks | 10,000 | 400 | 4% |
| Latest complete four weeks | 12,000 | 360 | 3% |

Clicks fell 10% while impressions rose 20%. That does not prove the page title failed. Check which queries gained appearances, which lost clicks and whether device or country mix changed. A new set of broad questions can lower overall click-through rate without changing the response to your most valuable service query.

Inspect relevant search results and the page itself. Record alternative explanations before editing anything. Then check actual inquiries: a small traffic decline and a decline in qualified demand are different business problems.

## Investigate indexing separately

Use URL Inspection when the question is whether Google has indexed the intended page. Compare the indexed information with the live test. Inspect the selected canonical and the page’s response, robots instructions, internal links and sitemap entry.

A successful live test is not a promise of indexing or a prediction of Google’s chosen canonical. Use the [canonical debugging guide](/blog/search-console-canonical-indexing-debugging/) when those signals disagree.

## Respect reporting limits

The [Performance report documentation](https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/7576553) explains filtering and data limits. Some queries are withheld for privacy, and displayed rows need not reconcile to every total. Do not manufacture the missing queries or call a filtered export the complete market.

Inspect the available report and its metric definitions rather than labelling all organic traffic as AI traffic. An AI impression does not establish a click, inquiry or sale.

## Leave with one documented action

Record the question, filters, comparison dates, observation, evidence, proposed change, owner and review date. For the example above, the next action might be to examine newly appearing broad queries before rewriting the service page.

After a repair, verify the actual page and allow for processing and recrawling before drawing conclusions. Keep an annotation for the change. If several changes happen together, acknowledge that the result cannot isolate the effect of one edit.

Use our [query and page review](/blog/search-console-query-page-review/) for the recurring routine. [Business intelligence](/services/business-intelligence/) connects these search observations with inquiry quality and operational records. The chart starts the investigation; it does not finish it.

[Download the fillable search review workbook](/downloads/search-review-workbook.pdf). It includes a worked comparison, space for your sources and decisions, and 12 acceptance checks. Keep unresolved questions with an owner and review date.

rewrite.title: How Long Does SEO Take? Track the Work and the Evidence
rewrite.markdown:
There is no reliable date on which SEO turns on. A technical correction, a new service page and a competitive market expansion have different dependencies.

You can still hold the work accountable. Agree on what will be delivered, what evidence should become available and when the next decision will be made. Keep those commitments separate from a promised ranking.

## Separate the stages

| Stage | What you can verify | What it does not prove |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Implementation | The agreed change is public and works | Google has processed it |
| Discovery | A crawler can reach the page through links or a sitemap | The page will be indexed |
| Indexing | The page appears in the indexed record | It will rank for the desired query |
| Search visibility | Relevant impressions and clicks appear | Those visitors are qualified customers |
| Business response | Valid inquiries or orders occur | SEO alone caused them |

Google's [guide to how Search works](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/how-search-works) explains crawling, indexing and serving as separate stages. Its [indexing request guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/ask-google-to-recrawl) makes clear that requesting a crawl does not guarantee inclusion.

## Set an initial delivery plan

In the first review period, expect a baseline, named priorities and evidence of completed work. If a service page is blocked or an inquiry form fails, the plan should identify an owner and acceptance test.

A reasonable plan may include business-fact verification, a sample of priority pages, technical corrections and a content brief. The exact sequence depends on the site. Do not replace a delivery plan with a vague instruction to wait six months.

## Worked example: an audit is not a deployment

Imagine an audit identifies incorrect canonical tags in January. The developer receives approval in February and releases the correction in March. The relevant implementation date is March, not the date the audit was emailed.

Record the affected URLs and inspect the public tags after release. Then check Google's indexed evidence as it becomes available. If the declared canonical is corrected but Google selects another URL, investigate equivalence and other signals instead of treating the task as automatically finished.

## Explain what is holding progress back

Useful questions include: Is the change awaiting approval? Is the page discoverable? Does it serve a distinct customer need? Is important evidence missing? Does the business have capacity to respond to inquiries? Are reporting definitions consistent?

A new business entering a competitive market may need substantial work and time to establish relevance and recognition. That is context for planning, not a reason to accept indefinite activity without evidence.

## Use monthly reviews to make decisions

Bring completed changes, validation, relevant search observations, qualified inquiries and unresolved dependencies. Compare suitable periods and label low-volume uncertainty. Preserve original publication dates; changing a date without a substantive update does not create better content.

If a core update overlaps the review, follow Google's [core update guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/core-updates) and avoid assigning every movement to your latest change.

## Agree on the next checkpoint

The next checkpoint should name the decision and required evidence: confirm indexability, assess a rewritten service page, or reconcile inquiry quality. It should not promise a position by an arbitrary date.

Use the [Search Console guide](/blog/google-search-console-the-operators-guide/) and [fillable review workbook](/downloads/search-review-workbook.pdf) to keep observations consistent. Good SEO reporting shows what happened, what remains uncertain and what happens next.

rewrite.title: SEO in 2026: What Deserves Your Attention
rewrite.markdown:
Search now includes more ways to encounter an answer than a list of website links. That changes what a business should observe. It does not remove the need for useful pages, accurate information and a working customer journey.

Use current platform documentation to distinguish a documented change from a proposed tactic. Keep experiments labelled as experiments.

## AI features use familiar foundations

Google's [AI features guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features) says supporting pages must be indexed and eligible for a snippet. It requires no special AI schema or new machine-readable text file.

Check whether important answers are accessible in the page, linked from relevant content and supported by evidence. Give each article a useful purpose. Do not create dozens of slight variations because a prompt tool can generate them quickly.

## Search access and training access are different decisions

OpenAI documents [separate search and training crawlers](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/bots). Do not change a site's training preference merely to make it discoverable in ChatGPT search.

A successful request with a copied bot user-agent does not establish genuine crawler access. Security controls may treat verified bot traffic differently. Use available server evidence or native inspection tools, and label what remains unverified.

For the practical implementation sequence, read the [AI-search visibility guide](/blog/ai-search-results-and-generative-search-optimization/).

## Reporting has changed; definitions still matter

Google's [June 2026 announcement](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2026/06/gen-ai-performance-reports) describes dedicated generative-AI visibility reports alongside overall performance reporting. Check the reports available in the actual property and read their metric definitions.

An impressions figure is not a separate count of AI-generated sales. Keep observed citations, identifiable referrals, valid inquiries and qualified leads distinct. Missing attribution should remain missing rather than being assigned to a fashionable channel.

## Content quality is not a detector score

Google's [spam policies](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies) address scaled content abuse. The useful review is whether the page adds value and makes accurate claims, not whether a detector guesses how a paragraph was drafted.

Read the article against its promise. A how-to should provide enough prerequisites, steps and validation for its audience. An analysis should separate evidence from interpretation. Verify author identity and remove experiences or results the author cannot substantiate.

## Worked priority decision

Imagine a business has an elaborate AI text file but a service page with an outdated phone number, unsupported claims and no clear inquiry route. Correct the business facts and buyer journey first. Then verify crawling and indexing, improve the supporting answers and record search observations.

The text file may remain a useful navigation aid. It is not evidence that any search system has indexed or cited the business.

## What to stop buying on faith

Be cautious with guaranteed AI placement, fabricated authority scores, bulk city pages and date changes presented as content refreshes. Ask what the proposed work changes, what source supports the claim and how its result can be observed.

Use service-aligned blog categories to organize distinct articles. Connect related guidance to relevant services without forcing every paragraph into a sales pitch. The [content hub workbook](/blog/build-a-content-hub-people-can-use/) provides the planning structure.

## Leave the review with an action

Choose one verified defect or useful improvement, name its owner and define completion. [Download the search review workbook](/downloads/search-review-workbook.pdf) for a record of sources, checks and follow-up. Review search visibility and business response over time; neither is established by publishing the change.

rewrite.title: Duplicate Content: Choose the Right Canonical or Redirect
rewrite.markdown:
Two URLs showing the same page are not automatically a penalty. They are a reason to check which URL should represent that content.

Google [selects a canonical](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/canonicalization) from pages it considers duplicate or very similar. Your preferred URL is a signal in that process, not a command. The practical question is whether the selected page is the right one for customers and your site.

## Identify the kind of duplication

Start with examples, not a site-wide replacement rule. Gather the affected URL, its preferred counterpart, response status, canonical tag, internal links and sitemap entry. If you have Search Console access, record the Google-selected canonical and the date of the indexed information.

| Situation | Appropriate starting point | What to verify |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tracking parameters show the same product | Canonical to the clean equivalent URL | The same product and content remain available |
| An old article has moved permanently | Redirect to its actual replacement | The destination answers the same need |
| Two distinct products share manufacturer copy | Improve their distinguishing information | Each product can still have its own useful page |
| A filtered collection serves a useful buying need | Evaluate it as a distinct landing page | Product selection, intent and page value differ |
| A utility page should not appear in Search | Consider noindex while allowing crawling | The page is not private; access controls protect private content |

A matching title alone does not prove two pages are duplicates.

![Choose a canonical for equivalent pages, a redirect for a permanent replacement, and preserve distinct useful pages.](/media/blog-review/canonical-decisions.svg)

## Canonicals are for equivalent content

Suppose the same blue backpack appears at a clean product URL and at that URL with a campaign parameter. A canonical pointing to the clean product URL can express your preference while both links continue to work.

A collection of backpacks is different from one backpack’s product page. Do not canonicalize the product to the collection because both mention backpacks. That discards the distinction the buyer needs.

Google’s [canonical guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/consolidate-duplicate-urls) explains the available signals. Keep your canonical, internal links and sitemap consistent. Use an absolute canonical URL that resolves successfully and represents the equivalent content.

## Redirect when the old address is no longer needed

If an article has permanently moved, a direct permanent redirect helps visitors and search systems reach the replacement. Check that the destination is relevant and that the redirect does not loop or pass through unnecessary intermediate URLs.

Do not redirect every deleted product or article to the homepage. When no useful replacement exists, an honest not-found response may be the appropriate result. See Google’s [redirect documentation](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/301-redirects).

## Treat filters and archives deliberately

A sort order may present the same collection differently. A carefully selected product subset can answer a different buying question. Inspect representative URLs before deciding how a filter family should be crawled or indexed.

Do not combine robots blocking, noindex and canonical tags indiscriminately. A crawler generally needs access to read a page’s indexing and canonical instructions. Google’s [faceted navigation guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/crawling-managing-faceted-navigation) discusses crawl management for large parameter spaces; that is a different question from choosing a representative among equivalent pages.

## Syndicated articles need an explicit agreement

When another publisher republishes an article, agree which copy should be eligible for Search before distribution. For syndicated material, Google [does not recommend relying on a canonical annotation](https://support.google.com/news/publisher-center/answer/9606800) to prevent duplication. Ask the partner about appropriate indexing restrictions and clear source attribution.

That is a publishing agreement, not a tag you can add to someone else’s website.

## Check the correction

After changing one representative URL, inspect its response, canonical, links and sitemap. Test the customer journey too. Then inspect the relevant Search Console result after Google has had a chance to recrawl; the live test does not predict Google’s eventual canonical choice.

Keep a simple record: affected URL, intended representative, reason, change, test result and follow-up date. Use the [canonical debugging walkthrough](/blog/search-console-canonical-indexing-debugging/) for a step-by-step investigation.

For repeated problems, fix the template, app or routing rule that creates them rather than editing hundreds of pages individually. [Technical SEO](/services/seo/) should leave a consistent site behind, not a spreadsheet full of exceptions.

## Keep a review record

[Download the fillable search review workbook](/downloads/search-review-workbook.pdf). It includes a worked comparison, space for your sources and decisions, and 12 acceptance checks. Keep unresolved questions with an owner and review date.
